definition.text: The branch of economics that studies the supply, demand and sharing out of the Earth's natural resources.

facts.text: A main aim is to understand nature's role in the economy so resources can be managed sustainably and stay available for future generations.
Its focus is how to run an economy within the ecological limits of the Earth's natural resources.
The traditional curriculum centred on fisheries, forestry and mineral extraction models: fish, trees and ore.
More recently air, water, the global climate and environmental resources in general have become important to policy, and interest has moved beyond optimal commercial exploitation alone.
Its traditional topics include welfare theory, land use, pollution control, resource extraction, non-market valuation, exhaustibility and sustainability.
The subfield began when researchers were mainly concerned with optimal commercial exploitation of natural resource stocks; environmental economics was once distinct from it.
Ecological economics criticises resource economics for focusing mainly on efficient allocation and less on fair distribution and the scale of the economy.

title: Stages of mineral resource development

definition.text: Vogely's five stages through which a mineral resource is developed, from the current operating margin to the technology margin.

facts.text: The five margins are the current operating margin, the intensive development margin, the extensive development margin, the exploration margin and the technology margin.
The Gray–Hotelling exhaustion theory covers only the first three stages, not the more important exploration and technology margins.

notes: Single-author scheme mentioned only on Natural resource economics; may fail curriculum tests.

title: Perpetual resource
article: Natural resource economics#Trend towards perpetual resources

definition.text: A resource so large relative to demand that it is unlikely ever to run out on a human time scale.

facts.text: Whether a resource is perpetual changes with new technology, new needs and new prices, plus how recyclable a material is and whether substitutes exist.
More efficient recovery lowers the ore grade needed: average processed copper ore fell from 4.0% copper in 1900 to 0.44% in 2000.
Salt, stone, magnesium and common clay have perpetual resources, and new technology added synthetic diamonds to the list.
Simon claimed the supply of natural resources is infinite, that is, perpetual.

title: Paleoresource
article: Natural resource economics#Transitioning: perpetual resources to paleoresources

definition.text: A resource for which there is little or no demand any more because the material taken from it has gone out of use.

facts.text: The classic example is arrowhead-grade flint, which nobody needs now that sharpened scrap steel is simpler.
US anthracite production fell from 70.4 million tonnes in 1905 to 1.5 million tonnes in 2005, so its reserves are now more than perpetual.
Decline reinforces itself: as customers switch fuels, dealers and then mines lose too much sales volume to cover costs and close.

definition.text: Replacing a scarce material with another one in its end uses, a main way economies escape shortages of a particular resource.

facts.text: Most mineral resources can be stretched by recycling and by substitutes for the end-use products.
Tin scarcity eventually led aluminium foil to replace tin foil, and polymer-lined steel cans and aseptic packaging to replace tin-plated cans.
When a 1978 invasion disrupted cobalt supply and briefly tripled its price, nickel and other substitutes were used instead.
Substitution and recycling can influence demand for minerals and so their availability.

definition.text: Any payment to the owner of a factor of production, such as land, beyond what is needed to bring that factor into use.

facts.text: Classical economists saw rent as payment for non-produced inputs such as land and location, or for privileges such as patents.
Rent is seen as unearned income, unlike economic profit, and competition cannot eliminate it.
In farming and extraction, economic rent arises from the scarcity and uneven spread of natural resources such as land, oil and minerals.
Scarcity rent is what is paid for identical land when supply is short of demand; differential rent is the surplus from better land over the poorest land in use.
Governments can collect part of resource rent as royalties or extraction fees on minerals, oil and gas.
Henry George argued that taxing unearned land rent would not distort economic activity and proposed it as the main source of public revenue.
Since the late 1800s the term has had several conflicting definitions, often used interchangeably, causing considerable confusion.
Public choice theorists later used rent for wealth transferred through state-granted rights, the source of the term rent seeking.

definition.text: A short-run, rent-like return earned by a factor of production, such as a machine or building, whose supply is fixed for the time being.

facts.text: Alfred Marshall developed the idea to extend rent reasoning from land to durable man-made factors fixed in supply in the short period.
Unlike pure rent, quasi-rent rewards the action needed to earn it, and in the long run it is competed away as new capital enters.
